articles.title: [Mind The Gap] Buyer’s remorse on Trump? Vote your pocketbook!
articles.summary: Sitting on the sidelines is no longer an option because our families here and back home are paying the price. Every vote counts.

blocks.text: When I gas up now, it’s past $6 a gallon for regular gasoline, and if you’re a big rig trucker, diesel is over $9 a gallon in California. When I do my groceries at the Island Pacific supermarket, a pound of bok choy for my pork neck bone sinigang, the same bunch that cost 99 cents before, is $2.99 now, even with my 12% senior citizen discount on Tuesdays.

And it’s not just our wallet being emptied here. The oil shock from the Iran war is also wreaking havoc on our loved ones in the Philippines, even as they continue to wade through stagnant flood water from the Habagat, worsened by crumbling flood control infrastructure, some of them with retaining walls built without rebar. And with diesel nearly P100 a liter, or about $6.50 a gallon, jeepney drivers are on the streets demanding higher fares.

At a time when they need remittances the most, we’re the ones cutting back as we try squeezing our own budget to put food on the table first. Those who count on $400 a month now get $200, if we can spare it.

With the US accounting for about $15 billion or 40% of all cash remittances to the Philippines every year, the whole country feels it when we pull back, with the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas already forecasting remittance growth to slow to 2.7% in 2026, down from 3.3% in 2025.

People say voters vote with their pocketbook. “It’s the economy, stupid!” — the line from Democratic strategist James Carville that helped win Clinton the presidency in ’92 — feels almost quaint now. But it’s happening again. Millions of Americans are struggling with the high cost of living, and just like the Iran war, there seems no end in sight to rising prices.

If you voted for Trump, that’s okay, nobody’s perfect. But you didn’t vote for higher prices, never asked for endless international conflicts even with our close allies, and never wanted Republicans in Congress to introduce a bill curtailing our immigration right to petition our own elderly parents.
Nor we imagined that our US citizenship can be revoked when audited for trivial mistakes, like a misstatement at the time of our application.

Because Filipinos have one of the highest naturalization rates — roughly 1.6 million, or 76% of our population — we are mathematically more likely to be caught in this arbitrary audit, with the United States Customs and Immigration Services (USCIS) setting a quota of 100 to 200 cases a month to strip citizenship from naturalized Americans in 2026.
Besides, Trump’s core support is showing deep fractures even among his MAGA faithful, especially those in Red States affected by the cost of tariffs and diesel fuel.

“Donald Trump is dragging down Republicans, even in some of the most Trump-y states,” according to New York Times contributing writer E.J. Dionne Jr. after reporting in Indiana and Kansas, where Trump’s approval is down in the 40s in both states.

While it’s impossible to argue with the rabid, Charlie Kirk-quoting Pinoy MAGAs, we have a potent voting bloc of the undecided and the disillusioned that can swing battleground states like Nevada where presidential and Senate races are routinely decided by thin margins.

Furthermore, while California is reliably blue, there are highly competitive US House districts across the Central Valley, Orange County, and parts of Los Angeles and San Diego. Since 41% of FilIpino eligible voters live in California, a surging turnout could help flip or hold the seats that can determine control of Congress.

Add to this the nearly 50 million Gen Zers ages 18 to 29 who will be eligible to vote this November, with more of them were registered as of July than at this point before the last midterm. Though more than 21 million eligible Gen Zers didn’t vote in 2024, their top concern now is the economy, which gives them a reason to show up.

Though there are more than four million Filipinos in the US, second only to the Chinese, we’ve been fence-sitters for so long in American politics that we’ve allowed those who came here after us, like the Indians and the Vietnamese, to gain a political clout we can now only dream of.

It could be apathy, why we are underrepresented in American politics. Our reluctance to take risks while sitting pretty on relative affluence from good-paying jobs made us lazy and indifferent to sort of flex our political power in terms of our large numbers.

We have often voted as individuals rather than organizing as a collective force, like in donating to candidates, which Indians generously do, or in walking the precincts or manning phone banks for our own kababayan running for office, or join protest rallies to support our rights as immigrants.

This midterm election, sitting on the sidelines is no longer an option because our families here and back home are paying the price. Every vote counts. As the Emperor in “Mulan” says, “a single grain can tip the scale.”
Let’s vote our pocketbook in November. – Rappler.com
Oscar Quiambao is a former reporter for The Philippine Daily Inquirer who now lives in San Francisco.

articles.title: [OPINYON] Para sa iyo, estudyanteng Inglesero
articles.summary: Kailangan natin ang mas maraming magtataguyod ng Filipino hindi lámang sa malikhaing pagsulat at sining. Kailangan natin ng mahuhusay na engineer, mathematician, philosopher, chemist, physicist, at…

blocks.text: Sorry, dude, pare, chong, bro.
Hindi ako sorry na magfi-Filipino sa pagkausap sa iyo ngayon.
Nabalitaan ko na di na raw ganoong nagfi-Filipino sa maraming pribadong paaralan natin. Kompara noong panahon ko circa early 2000s. Oo, may pinagkatandaan na rin pala ako.
Kailangan ko sigurong mag-under-cover sa mga sumunod na araw para malaman kung totoo talaga itong penomenon na ito na naghari na ang English-Only Policy.

Pero kung totoo talaga ito, una ko nang sasabihin na isang malaking kawalan sa sinumang estudyante kung hindi ka magiging mahusay sa Filipino. Isang bentaha o advantage ang pagiging bilingual. Minimum ang pagiging bilingual. Kayâ magbabahagi lang din ako ng kaunting danas tungkol sa sariling pagtataguyod ng ating wika.

Tulad ninyo, sabi nila, trademark daw ng ilang mga paaralan ang Ingles nila. Narinig ko na ito sa isang kaibigang babae noong undergrad pa ako sa isang paaralan sa España. Siyempre, kapag una mong narinig, ipagmamalaki mo. Wow, may sariling paraan pala kami ng pag-i-Ingles na mahusay.

Pero saan ba táyo nadala ng husay na iyon? Para sa ating tagumpay sa mas mataas na edukasyon? Para makakuha ng magandang trabaho? Para kapag nag-alumni homecoming ay magyayabangan tayo sa isa’t isa at mag-i-Inglesan? Naisip ko ulit na hindi rin naman pala mga konyo ang ka-batch ko. Wagas nga ang pagfi-Filipino namin. Sagad sa buto ang mga mura, biruan, at pangangatwiran.
Sana matanong ninyo rin sa hinaharap para masagot ito: Ingles lámang ba ang makatutulong para maging mabuting mga Filipino táyo ngayon at sa hinaharap?
Samantalang may wika táyo na itinaguyod ng mga nauna sa atin para tugunan iyon: ang maging mas mabuti at mahusay na Filipino.

Bakit? Dahil mas maiintindihan táyo ng mga kapuwa natin kapag ginamit natin ito. Sa trabaho ko bilang mananaliksik ng wika at kultura, nalibot ko na rin ang Filipinas at masasabi ko sa inyo na nagkakaunawaan kami ng kausap ko na Lambangian gáling Magindanaw o Itnëg mulang Abra kapag ginamit namin ang Filipino sa harap ng mga pagkakaiba namin sa wika. At, siyempre, nagtatangka rin akong matutuhan ang mga wika nila kahit kakaunti lámang ang ibinigay na panahon.

Haharapin mo rin ito kapag lumabas ka na rito sa iyong pugad ng pribilehiyo. Malamang magtutungo ka sa unibersidad na default ang wikang Ingles. Tandaan mo, default lang, at puwedeng-puwede mong gamitin pa rin ang wikang pambansa natin. At paglabas sa mga unibersidad patungo sa mga alternatibong unibersidad ng mga pamayanan nating dapat paglingkuran, makikita mo na hindi naman umiikot sa Ingles ang bayan natin.

Kayâ habang bata ka pa, kailangan mong malaman na kailangan natin ang mas maraming magtataguyod ng Filipino hindi lámang sa malikhaing pagsulat at sining. Higit pa rito, kailangan natin ng mahuhusay na engineer, mathematician, philosopher, chemist, physicist, at iba pang mga propesyonal na gagamitin ang ating wikang pambansa.

Pangarap natin kasi iyon sa wika natin, ang maging isang intelektuwalisadong wika tulad ng Ingles, Japanese, Spanish, German, atbpa. Intellectualized kasi ginagamit sa iba’t ibang field para lumikha ng karunungan. Intellectualized kasi araw-araw ginagamit ng mga user nito at hindi lámang tuwing Buwan ng Wika.

Hámon ko po sa iyo ito, estudyanteng Inglesero: magpakahusay ka sa Filipino. At sakâ, kilalanin at aralin mo ang mga wika ng iyong magulang at lolo’t lola na nagsasalita ng Ilokano, Sebwano, Hiligaynon, Ivatan, atbpa. Kayamanan at angat ang pag-iisip ng isang táong hindi lámang isa ang nalalamang wika.

Bakit? Kapag higit sa isang wika, higit sa isang paraan ng pag-iisip at kultura ang nabubuksan sa isip mo. Matututuhan mong hindi lámang pag-iisip ng mga Amerikano o Britong nag-i-Ingles ang umiiral. Mayroon din táyong sarili sa Filipino, meron din táyong maraming magkakaugnay at magkakaibang sarili sa ating 137 katutubong wika.

Kayâ sa pagtatapos, gusto ko lang ding magpugay sa mga naging guro ko sa Filipino sa aking munting paaralan sa Shaw Boulevard na sina Ginang Lumanog at Binibining Rarang. Kasama na rin sina Sir Jepoy at Sir VJ, na nagturo sa akin ng kasaysayan sa sariling wika. Kung babalikan ko nga, dapat mas pinagbuti ko pa sa kanilang klase. Kasi, tulad mo, feel na feel ko rin na sa Ingles lang ako dapat maging magaling dati. – Rappler.com

Sumusulat si Roy Rene S. Cagalingan ng mga tula at sanaysay. Kasapi siya ng Linangan sa Imahen, Retorika, at Anyo (LIRA) at Unyon ng mga Manunulat sa Pilipinas (UMPIL). Naglilingkod siya sa Komisyon sa Wikang Filipino (KWF).

articles.title: EU ministers mull new ways to curb irregular migration
articles.summary: The proposals include setting up so-called return hubs outside the EU and strengthening the border agency Frontex. Greece has even proposed temporarily suspending asylum applications in emergency…

image.caption: The EU wants to implement tougher migration policies centered on border controls, deterrence and returns [FILE: April 5, 2019]Image: picture-alliance/NurPhoto/N. Economou

blocks.text: The interior ministers of European Union countries met in Luxembourg on Thursday to discuss ways to strengthen border controls and curb undocumented migration into the 27-member bloc.
Following the talks, they approved a new regulation to boost deportations of irregular migrants.
It will allow member states ​to establish so-called return hubs outside the EU for migrants who are legally required to leave the bloc but cannot be returned to their countries of origin.
Countries including Denmark, Austria, Greece, Germany and the Netherlands have been exploring options to change migration policy and set up such migrant centers.
How the far right hardened Europe's migration stance
What did the ministers say?
"When it comes to return hubs," Danish Interior Minister Morten Bodskov told reporters, "it's progressing very well."
"We are moving in the right direction," he said without providing further details.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said there were "preliminary" talks on return hubs but declined to say which countries were involved.
More work was needed to make sure any agreement would withstand possible lawsuits, he said.
"These agreements are meant to be sustainable in the long term," Dobrindt noted, adding that he was nevertheless hopeful that a first deal could be sealed by the end of the year.
Dutch Migration Minister Bart van den Brink said a technical mission already visited a potential host country in early September.
Supporters of the policy say return hubs could facilitate repatriations and act as a deterrent for would-be irregular migrants.
But critics question their legality and argue that they violate migrants' fundamental rights.
Spain: Tensions in aftermath of Ceuta mass migrant crossing
Suspending asylum process in emergencies?
On Thursday, Greece even proposed temporarily suspending asylum applications in emergency situations. The right to seek asylum is guaranteed by the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights.
Athens argued that current rules are inadequate to handle mass arrivals as in Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta this summer.

The Spanish government estimates over 72,000 migrants entered Ceuta in late July. While most of them have since returned, some 10,000 remain, reinforcing calls in some EU capitals for a tougher approach. The Spanish government has said only minors and small groups of the people who entered Ceuta were brought to mainland Spain.
Greece's proposal appeared to draw support from some member states.

"We have to find a legal way not to bring them into the asylum procedure," said Dutch Migration Minister van den Brink. "In situations like Ceuta, it should be treated as ​a border management issue rather than an asylum issue."

Asked whether he saw a suspension of asylum as possible under the new emergency law, ​Magnus Brunner, EU commissioner for migration, said: "Europe needs the means to protect its borders at all times," while stressing that "we will always comply with fundamental rights and values."
How the EU compromised its values on migration
Plans to curtail irregular migration
The interior ministers' talks come as undocumented migration remains high on the EU's political agenda, with far-right parties increasingly gaining support across the bloc.
The situation has pushed many governments towards tougher migration policies centered on border controls, deterrence and returns.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said this month that the Commission will propose an emergency tool for countries to better deal with mass migration movements.
But details are still being worked out.
There are also plans to strengthen the EU's border agency, Frontex, with many stressing the need for the organization to have a rapid intervention force that could intervene in border crises.

articles.title: Have P5,000? You can invest in RTB 32 and earn 6.8% per year
articles.summary: When the common public purchases these bonds, they are not merely performing a civic duty; they are securing a reliable, wealth-building vehicle to shield their savings from inflation and market…

blocks.text: Last Tuesday, September 29, the Bureau of Treasury (BTr) launched the public offering of its latest retail bond issue, the Retail Treasury Bonds Tranche 32 (RTB-32).

RTB-32 has a term of 2.5 years and features an attractive coupon rate of 6.875% per annum, with interest paid quarterly and subject to a 20% final withholding tax. The auction’s first day had an overwhelming oversubscription, raising P84.9 billion against an initial target of P30 billion.
To allow the high participation of the common public to become investors in the issue, the minimum investment requirement is P5,000 only.

Investors can subscribe over-the-counter through authorized selling banks or digitally via the BTr Online Ordering Facility, the LANDBANK Mobile Banking App, OFBank App, RCBC Pulz, ATRAM apps, PDAX, and GCash via its GBonds platform.
Additionally, investors holding specific older government securities can choose to swap them directly for RTB 32 before the final settlement of this new issue on October 12, 2026.

RTBs are considered powerful and stable, non-inflationary instrument used to fund national budgets, build infrastructure, and manage fiscal deficits. It is also one of the ideal instruments that could help promote financial inclusion and literacy to the general public, many of whom still remain with limited access to mainstream investment services.

In this regard, RTBs were actually the subject of discussion at the Monday Circle’s latest forum. Like always, the subject was given a critical eye on what it has been doing in financing the government and on its role in promoting savings and financial literacy.

Invited as guest speaker for the occasion was Director Robert Dominick “Doms” Mariano, head of the research department of the Bureau of Treasury (BTr). Mariano has more than 15 years of work experience on debt management, government finance, and fiscal programming. He also has an extensive background on national government treasury management, financial market surveillance, risk management, and macroeconomic and fiscal planning.
RTBs have gone a long way from a tradeable small-denominated bonds under the “Small Investors Program” in late 1998 into what it is now as a pillar of the country’s national debt management strategy.

Over the last 25 years, RTBs have transitioned from a niche financial inclusion project into a strategic financing instrument for the government. They have become the cornerstone for sovereign fund mobilization or the process by which the government gathers, pools, and deploys its financial resources at the same time serving as a practical, real-world classroom that elevates the financial literacy of the general public.

Today, RTBs are no longer a minor funding source. They consistently make up to roughly 35% of the government’s outstanding domestic debt securities. The government has been intentionally utilizing RTBs to protect the national budget from extreme foreign exchange shocks and global market volatility.

RTBs became a critical crisis-management tool during the COVID-19 pandemic. The government leaned heavily on its RTB-25 and RTB-26 bond issues to strategically raise billions for pandemic response programs and health infrastructure.

The regular distribution model of RTBs teaches the mechanics of passive income and cash flow management because RTBs pay out interest on a fixed, quarterly basis. When an ordinary saver receives a direct credit to their account every three months, the concept of “money working for you” transitions from a textbook phrase into a tangible reality.

Moreover, this predictable structure teaches individuals how to budget around recurring income streams, encouraging long-term financial planning over impulsive short-term spending. Thus, RTBs are the perfect beginner tool for financial literacy for the common public.

Again, when the government launches an educational roadshow or a financial literacy webinar to explain how an RTB works, it is not doing it as a formality only. It is actively promoting these bonds to raise the money the country needs.

Conversely, when the common public purchases these bonds, they are not merely performing a civic duty; they are securing a reliable, wealth-building vehicle to shield their savings from inflation and market volatility.

This process creates a chain reaction where one good thing leads to another. As government outreach increases public awareness, the general saving public becomes more financially literate. A more financially literate population, in turn, demands a higher volume of secure, transparent investment products, driving deeper demand for subsequent government bond issuances.

Over time, this collaborative mechanism fosters a robust domestic capital market, reduces the national dependency on foreign debt, and builds a financially resilient society capable of weathering macroeconomic shocks.

As summarized by Mariano, the RTB program illustrates that sound fiscal policy and public financial empowerment are not competing priorities, but mutually reinforcing pillars of long-term economic development. They are a powerful economic bridge that balances the government’s financial needs with the public’s wealth goals.

By offering a safe, high-yielding alternative to standard savings, RTBs gather scattered public money to fund critical infrastructure. At the same time, they open up the financial world to everyone, transforming the common public into disciplined, smart, and tech-savvy investors. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Trump threatens to hit Iran 'very hard' if Tehran found to be behind FlyDubai incident
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday that if Iran is linked to the copilot who tried to crash an Israel-bound flight, the Islamic Republic would be struck "very hard" for the attempt on the…

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump speaks at an event in Denton, Texas, on Thursday. (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday that if Iran is linked to the copilot who tried to crash an Israel-bound flight, the Islamic Republic would be struck "very hard" for the attempt on the lives of more than 180 people aboard the jet.
Investigators still working to determine cause after co-pilot stabbed captain

U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday that if Iran is linked to the co-pilot who tried to crash an Israel-bound flight, the Islamic Republic would be hit "very hard" over the attempt on the lives of more than 180 people aboard the jet.

Trump issued the warning as investigators worked to determine why the co-pilot stabbed the flight's captain, causing the FlyDubai plane to plummet before others on board stopped the attack and landed the airliner in Saudi Arabia.
The president was asked by reporters at the White House whether he had been briefed about any links between the co-pilot behind the attack and Tehran.
"We're working on it right now," Trump said. "I would say the answer, based on what I'm hearing, is yes, but we're working on it right now."
Trump did not elaborate about why he suspects Iran might be involved.
India celebrates pilot who averted disaster on FlyDubai plane
Asked if the U.S. would retaliate against Tehran if it was behind the attack, Trump said, "Oh they'll be hit, very hard, don't worry."
"You just ask them," he said. "They know what happened. They'll be hit very hard."
Stalled diplomacy
His remarks came as diplomatic efforts to end the war appear to have stalled.

Iranian officials indicated Wednesday that they had received an official U.S. response to Tehran's latest proposal to end the seven-month war, which Trump had publicly rejected just days earlier. The officials did not say what the response contained and whether it was a rejection.

items: Trump rejects Iranian proposal to open Strait of Hormuz and end fighting

blocks.text: Trump said in a Time magazine interview published Thursday that he would not accept proposals from Iran that "he wouldn't have approved a year ago," and left open the possibility of resuming bombing after the Nov. 3 U.S. election.

Meanwhile, the U.S. military has dispatched roughly 9,000 troops aboard a group of ships to the Middle East, a U.S. official said Thursday. That could mean three aircraft carriers will be in the region as soon as late October, according to the official, who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military operations.

Despite Trump's public rebuff, mediators have continued working with Iran and the U.S. to try to broker a deal to end the fighting and open the Strait of Hormuz, according to officials who were not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity.

articles.title: Enter Shikari announce indefinite hiatus from 2027: ‘We don’t think we’re splitting up’
articles.summary:
Rock band will still tour the UK, Europe and US over the next year but say decision to ‘fall dormant’ feels ‘liberating’

The British rock band Enter Shikari have announced they will go on…

blocks.text: The British rock band Enter Shikari have announced they will go on hiatus at the end of 2027, a decision that may result in the band’s “extinction”.
The St Albans band, who formed in 1999 as Hybryd, are due to tour the UK in November, Europe and the US next year, and said they hoped to play some of their favourite places “one last time”.

A statement from band reads: “As of December 31, 2027, Enter Shikari will fall dormant as a recording and performing entity. This dormancy may eventually end with an eruption back into activity, or may end with extinction, we have no idea which.

“As everyone keeps reminding us, 2027 will be 20 years since the release of our debut album. We’ve been playing music together since we were 15, and friends longer still, but there’s no doubt this is a huge milestone.

“For the past two decades, we’ve run amok in a cultural landscape that elevates easily-pigeonholed art, so being an Enter Shikari hasn’t always been easy, professionally or personally, with obvious negative impact on one’s mental health when tasked with coming up with the goods.

“But we do this because we love it, and we are lucky enough to have built an audience who understand that the less-trodden path is sometimes the more interesting journey. However, it gets to the point where the often difficult terrain of that path starts to frazzle and drain the humble traveller.

“We are far from being the same kids who recorded that debut album, and as much as we love what we do, and still love being in each other’s company, as humans our priorities and capacities have changed.”
The band said their lead singer, Rou Reynolds, had suffered “recent illness” but they had already had “difficult conversations” about their future before that.

“To then see a friend in trouble made those conversations more pertinent,” the statement reads. “While we don’t think we’re splitting up, we do not have a diary that extends beyond 2027 … Maybe we’ll be like Fugazi and just get together to rehearse for fun, without feeling the need to make anyone else listen to it.
“All we really know is after two decades of being a professional band, not having plans three years in advance is liberating.”
The band also said they were working on new music, which fans “should get to hear sooner rather than later, along with another thing we’ve just finished filming”.
Enter Shikari added that they would not be announcing a “farewell world tour”.
The statement concludes: “It’s not the sort of statement we thought we’d be making if you’d asked us a year ago, but we felt it was time to let you know our headspace.
“We really hope we’ll be seeing you over the next 14 months or so, somehow. But if not, all that remains to be said is thank-you for your support, your sweat, your passion, your energy.”
Since forming in 1999, the band have released six UK top 10 albums, including a No 1 with A Kiss for the Whole World in 2023.
They have also scored a handful of hit singles including Anything Can Happen in the Next Half, Juggernauts and Sssnakepit.

articles.title: Joshua Kutryk's launch to the ISS is another example of the important role Canada plays in space exploration
articles.summary: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk blasted off to the International Space Station for a six-month mission just a few months after fellow Canadian Jeremy Hansen flew around the moon. It's an example of…

image.caption: The SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket and Dragon spacecraft lifts off Thursday morning with Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk on board. (Philip Scott Andrews/Reuters)

blocks.text: Science·Analysis

Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk blasted off to the International Space Station for a six-month mission just a few months after fellow Canadian Jeremy Hansen flew around the moon. It's an example of not only Canada's continuing role in space exploration but also how bright the future could be.
'It's been a big year, a big year for Canada,' says Industry Minister Mélanie Joly
Canadian Joshua Kutryk is in space, on his way to the International Space Station (ISS) after a flawless launch from Cape Canaveral, Fla.
The SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket blasted off at 11:10 a.m., right on time.
He and his crewmates — NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, and Russian cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov — are slated to dock with the ISS after roughly eight hours in space.

items: Crew-13 astronauts, including Canada's Joshua Kutryk, on their way to dock with ISS

blocks.text: The launch is Kutryk's first, and he felt it.
"I'm in space. I don't really believe it yet. It does feel weird, though," he said. "It's good to be here."
'It does feel weird': Canadian astronaut on entering space

This is a historic moment for Canada. It's the first time two Canadians have launched into space in such a short time. Jeremy Hansen launched as part of NASA's Artemis II mission for a trip around the moon only six months ago.
Minister of Industry Mélanie Joly was at the NASA press site shortly after the launch and noted the important role Canada has played and can play in space.

items: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk is in 'high spirits' for Thursday's launch to the International Space Station

blocks.text: "It's been a big year, a big year for Canada," she said.

"And now we look forward to seeing how Josh Kutryk's work will continue to obviously participate in international efforts about space exploration and space co-operation, but also to inspire so many young Canadians and older ones that are very much fascinated by space."
Canada's continuing role
Undoubtedly, there have been tensions between Canada and the U.S., but not when it comes to space.

While it's true that NASA has cancelled Lunar Gateway, which would have included Canadarm3, it wasn't due to any political strain between our two countries. Rather, it was a shift in mission priorities brought forth by NASA administrator Jared Isaacman.

Earlier this year, Isaacman announced that NASA was adding a mission to the Artemis Program, which aims to return humans to the lunar surface by 2028. And that resulted in the cancellation of the lunar space station and a focus on constructing a lunar base.
Asked by the CBC at the post-launch news conference about Canada's collaboration with NASA in its future plans, Isaacman hinted that Canada could play a vital role in the future of a lunar base.
"Canada has immense expertise in robotics, clearly, as demonstrated from the Canadarm performance from shuttle to the ISS," he said.

"As the base becomes operational, it should almost be the last choice to send somebody outside in that very demanding and dangerous environment. And you're going to need extensive robotic capabilities … and we're going to be counting on it as part of the architecture."

items: This medical device heading to space with Joshua Kutryk is also helping people here on Earth

blocks.text: It's not only robotics that Canada is looking to contribute, but also lunar rovers.

In December 2025, the CSA awarded four Canadian organizations with contracts totalling $3.2 million for the development of a lunar utility rover that would be used for science, transportation and more to support astronauts on the lunar surface. (Unfortunately, in March the CSA announced the cancellation of another, smaller rover that would have conducted scientific missions on the moon.)
Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk lifts off for 6-month ISS mission

"We want to play a bigger part in everything linked to space exploration, but particularly with the moon," Joly said on Thursday. "Being able to have more of a Canadian presence, particularly on the robotic side."
Part of Isaacman's Artemis program restructuring included the speeding up of launches in the Artemis program.
On Thursday, Joly said Canada is ready.
"We know that NASA wants to go further, faster," she said. "We want to do more of that."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Based in Toronto, Nicole covers all things science for CBC News. As an amateur astronomer, Nicole can be found looking up at the night sky appreciating the marvels of our universe. She is the editor of the Journal of the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada and the author of several books. In 2021, she won the Kavli Science Journalism Award from the American Association for the Advancement of Science for a Quirks and Quarks audio special on the history and future of Black people in science. You can send her story ideas at nicole.mortillaro@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Montreal hospital isolates patient exhibiting Ebola symptoms
articles.summary: A Montreal hospital has isolated a female patient presenting with symptoms of Ebola, a deadly virus, officials said.

image.caption: A CHUM spokesperson said all necessary safety measures have been put in place and stressed that there are currently no concerns regarding public exposure. (Hugo Therrien/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Montreal·New
A Montreal hospital has isolated a female patient presenting with symptoms of Ebola, a deadly virus, officials said.
Hospital says there are currently no concerns regarding public exposure

articles.title: Trump's trade rep sounds pessimistic about deal with Canada, saying issues are 'quite difficult to resolve'
articles.summary: U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer says he regularly speaks with his Canadian counterpart, but that the two sides have reached an impasse on some trade irritants and there's no sign of a…

image.caption: U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer speaks during the second day of the G20 Trade Ministerial Conference at the Pfister Hotel in Milwaukee on Thursday. (Kamil Krzaczynski/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer says he regularly speaks with his Canadian counterpart, but that the two sides have reached an impasse on some trade irritants and there's no sign of a resolution any time soon.
Jamieson Greer says while 'technical talks' are ongoing, there are 'a handful of outstanding issues'
· CBC News
· Posted: Oct 01, 2026 7:01 PM EDT | Last Updated: 27 minutes ago

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer says he regularly speaks with his Canadian counterpart, but the two sides have reached an impasse on some trade irritants and there's no sign of a resolution any time soon.

Speaking to reporters at the G20 meeting of trade ministers in Milwaukee, Greer sounded pessimistic about the prospect of a deal with the Canadians saying while "technical talks" are ongoing between trade experts from both countries there are some fundamental disagreements.
"The reality is there are a handful of outstanding issues that are quite difficult to resolve," Greer said.
Greer said the Trump administration's policy of imposing tariffs on foreign manufactured goods to try to "reindustrialize" America is a universal one and not "focused on one country."

items: Trump says 'very bad' Canada is being 'taught a little lesson' as trade action escalates

blocks.text: Canada, meanwhile, maintains that punishing tariffs on industrial products like steel, aluminum and autos make no sense given just how integrated the two economies are after decades of free trade.

The federal government has strenuously opposed U.S. tariffs designed to decimate those key Canadian sectors, saying it's no way to treat a supposed ally. Plus, Canada is America's biggest customer, purchasing more American-exported goods than any other country.
U.S. losing manufacturing jobs

Still, Greer said Canada and other countries treat the United States as "a dumping ground" for their products and the U.S. just wants to produce more of what it consumes domestically. He added that these policies shouldn't be read as "threats against Canada" alone.

Despite Greer's claims that these tariff policies are boosting industrial employment, data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics compiled by the Economic Policy Institute shows that some some, 62,000 manufacturing jobs have been lost since Trump took office for his second term in January 2025.
Carney laughs at Trump's claim that Canada will apologize to U.S.
International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu, who is responsible for non-U.S. trade, met with Greer while in Wisconsin.

The conversation was focused primarily on wider world trade issues like ending forced labour and the phenomenon of some countries like China dumping heavily state-subsidized products into market economies.
But the Canada-U.S. dispute did come up, Sidhu said in an interview with CBC News.
He said he stressed to Greer that the two countries need to "find a way to work together, especially for our auto supply workers."
"I think there is energy from both sides," Sidhu said, calling it a "very cordial conversation."
"But we want a good deal," he said. "We won't accept anything less."
Greer downplays Trump's deal comments

Speaking earlier Thursday to Bloomberg News from the summit, Greer seemed to downplay President Donald Trump's assertion this week that the Canadians would come calling for a deal and that something could come together within a month.
"You've heard the president talk about this. Most recently he said, 'Well, we may have a deal with Canada in a few weeks.' I'd emphasize the 'may' in that part of the situation," Greer said.

items: Trump trade adviser says Canada will 'pay even more dearly' if 'you interfere' in U.S. midterms

blocks.text: Greer reiterated that the U.S. is open to a deal with Canada, but he suggested Prime Minister Mark Carney and his negotiators can't accept what the Americans are offering.

"The question is does Canada want to get to 'yes' on some of these things. We have a trade policy where we're not inclined to go to zero tariffs because we're trying to reshore," he said. "Gaps remain between Canada and the United States."

Those "gaps" became apparent when Canada-U.S. trade talks collapsed in August, with Carney pulling his negotiators back from Washington after what he described as a series of last-minute American changes that weren't workable for Canada.

Canada was concerned about U.S. tariffs on medium- and heavy-duty trucks, which could have made a GM plant in Oshawa, Ont., that produces Chevrolet Silverados uncompetitive and imperiled the planned production of Ford F-250s in Oakville, Ont.

items: Carney says trade deal became untenable when U.S. 'asked too much and offered too little'
Carney outlines the last-minute changes U.S. tacked onto trade deal terms

blocks.text: Carney also said he couldn't accept language in the proposed deal that could have compromised Canada's sovereignty, namely provisions he described as limiting the government's ability to make trade deals with other countries.
U.S. opposition to Canadian policies designed to promote the "discoverability" of French-language programming on streaming services was also an issue, Carney has said.

While Greer seemingly backed down from U.S. demands on French-language content in an interview with CBC News, no apparent progress has been made on those other issues in the weeks since the bilateral talks imploded.
Carney said this week he thinks it's possible to negotiate a "mutually advantageous trade arrangement" with the U.S. at some point in the future.
"Canada stands ready to negotiate in good faith," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

J.P. Tasker is a journalist in CBC's parliamentary bureau who reports for digital, radio and television. He is also a regular panellist on CBC News Network's Power & Politics. He covers the Conservative Party, Canada-U.S. relations, the Crown in Canada, health policy and the Senate. You can send story ideas and tips to J.P. at jp.tasker@cbc.ca

articles.title: Falling glass and ‘decapitated’ plants: the race to protect Edinburgh botanic garden’s plants
articles.summary:
After five years of work, 5,750 panels of toughened glass will help keep hundred of plants safe from Scottish winters – but more work needs to be done

In the early autumn sunlight, Royal…

blocks.text: In the early autumn sunlight, Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh’s extensive plant collection appears safe in their glass enclosures. But danger lurks from above for the tropical ferns, cycads and rare alpine heathers.

Soon the September sunshine will give way to the storms and gales of the Scottish winter, which can bring hundreds of glass panels crashing to the greenhouse floor on the windiest days. Nobody is allowed inside when the wind is above 30mph.

“We’ve had plants that have essentially been decapitated by falling bits of glass,” says Sadie Barber, the glasshouse curator at RBGE. “You go into one of these tropical spaces in winter and there’s icy air coming in. It’s traumatic for those of us who put decades into caring for these plants. A storm can literally just wipe them out.”

blocks.caption: Prof Julia Knights, regius keeper and CEO of RBGE, officially opening the doors. Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian

blocks.text: But this week, change is in the air for the creaking infrastructure at the 356-year-old botanic garden, the second oldest in Britain after Oxford. On Friday, the palm houses are reopening after five years of painstaking restoration work, complete with 5,750 panels of toughened glass to keep out the elements.

Before they closed for renovation works, the horticultural team had installed a net in case panels fell from the weathered structure. The new ones are not bulletproof – but they are strong enough to resist a bird strike.

blocks.caption: Damage to one of the glasshouses after a storm. Photograph: Helen Pugh Photography

blocks.text: Part-Georgian, part-Victorian, the £23.5m refurbishment has kept nearly all of the original sandstone and wrought iron shell. Inside, more than 600 temperate plants have returned to the building. The air is clean and crisp, purified by ferns that naturally remove toxins from the air. Its temperature and humidity is still controlled by the original pulleys and winches.

“We have made it one vast cathedral-like space for temperate plants,” says Prof Julia Knights, the garden’s regius Keeper and the royally appointed chief executive. She points out her favourite tree fern, which comes from Tasmania and has a Scottish liverwort growing on its woody stem. “They can grow outside in our botanic garden in Logan on the west coast of Scotland because of the oceanic climate,” she says.

blocks.caption: Extensive work has been done to replace and strengthen panels at the greenhouse. Photograph: Helen Pugh Photography

blocks.text: Founded by two physicians in 1670 to teach doctors about medicinal plants, RBGE has morphed into one of the most important collections of plant biodiversity in the world. Its research glasshouses are stuffed with rare ginger species, bananas, blueberries and dozens of begonias.

It is a global authority on rhododendrons and ferns, houses rare plant species that have gone extinct in the wild, and its scientists have helped pioneer new technology, such as DNA barcoding which is used to identify plant species. Arthur Conan Doyle studied here, infusing Sherlock Holmes novels with his botanical knowledge. Today, conservation is its primary focus.
after newsletter promotion

“Our conservation collections are so important to have. The threats are extreme in the wild,” said Prof Pete Hollingsworth, RBGE’s director of science. “The driver[s] for environmental damage are so strong, so having these ex situ safe sites is really important,” he said.

blocks.caption: New display benches in the restored building. Photograph: RBGE

blocks.text: But the restored palm houses aside, many of the glasshouses used to care for the plants are decades past their originally intended lifespan and are waiting for upgrades. Leaks from Scottish rain rot the rootstock of plants, sometimes killing them. Last year, horticulturalists were not allowed inside the greenhouses for 20 days due to high winds. In 2026, they have been shut out 15 times. When they return, they have often worn hard hats and safety gear to pick out the broken glass.

“The glasshouses are the one thing we don’t want to break. It’s the plants inside that suffer,” said Barber. “I was looking at one of our records the other day of a plant we lost in the lowland tropical house. It just had ‘storm’ written next to it. It had either suffered from the cold, or even been cut by falling glass.”

articles.title: New Washington DC law bans landlords from imposing dog breed restrictions
articles.summary:
Landlords can no longer refuse pit bulls, rottweilers, dobermans or other breeds considered ‘scary’

Landlords in Washington DC will no longer be able to refuse a tenant’s dog based on its…

blocks.text: Landlords in Washington DC will no longer be able to refuse a tenant’s dog based on its breed, size or weight, nor can they impose special charges related to these factors.

At least, that’s what a new law that took effect on Thursday aims to achieve. Animal welfare organizations and animal shelters applauded the legislation, emphasizing the benefits of reducing barriers to pet ownership in the US capital.

Dog breeds considered “scary” used to face restrictions, especially pit bulls, rottweilers and dobermans. Property owners could ban certain breeds, regardless of their behavior. With these restrictions, landlords tried to avoid incidents with aggressive dogs that could damage property or harm other tenants or pets.

However, animal groups challenged this claim, explaining that breed bans penalize responsible dog owners and that in the vast majority of cases, aggressive behavior is linked to owner management and control, and not to the dog’s breed. Also, they warned that exorbitant pet fees and breed restrictions were putting housing out of reach for people.

What takes effect this Thursday is the last part of the pets in housing amendment act, or “Roscoe’s Law”, brought forward by councilmember Robert White in honor of his dog. The first part has been partially in effect since 2025. It included caps on pet-related fees: under that first part of the legislation, pet security deposits cannot exceed 15% of a tenant’s monthly rent, pet rent is capped at 1% of the monthly rent, and all other non-refundable fees are prohibited.

While organizations like the DC Landlord Association acknowledged that the law’s intent “to help keep families together and prevent the separation of pets from their owners due to restrictive housing policies”, they expressed concerns. In May, they worried that the security deposits and rent caps included in the law might not cover the costs associated with pet-related damages, and called for “adequate” deposits and rent.

Although breed and weight restrictions are prohibited in all residential leases beginning after 1 October 2026, immediate changes may not be evident. Real estate websites commonly include pet restrictions on their property listings.

In a quick search on Zillow on Thursday, many “pet-friendly” DC listings included a “pet essentials” section where it stated if the property allowed cats or dogs and their weight limit, and it was sometimes set at a maximum of 75lb.

articles.title: US states and cities sue over Trump EPA’s repeal of emissions rules
articles.summary:
Democratic-led coalition says gutting key protections will set US back decades and worsen climate crisis

States and cities sued the Trump administration on Thursday for repealing rules that…

blocks.text: States and cities sued the Trump administration on Thursday for repealing rules that limit planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions from power plants fueled by coal and natural gas.

Twenty-one states, led by New York, are challenging the Environmental Protection Agency’s power plant rule. The Democratic-led coalition also includes Pennsylvania’s governor, the District of Columbia, New York City, Chicago and the city and county of Denver. They argue that “gutting one of the country’s most significant climate protections” will set the nation back decades and worsen the climate crisis.
The EPA announced last month it’s revoking the Biden-era rule, and said it is taking a separate but related step to prevent future administrations from regulating climate pollution from power plants.

New York attorney general Letitia James said the federal government is showing “callous disregard” for Americans’ health and the environment, and future generations will pay the price. Power plants that burn fossil fuels are a major source of planet-warming pollution.
“Dismantling these protections is a betrayal of American families, and the stakes are too high to allow this administration to once again put profits over people,” James said in a statement Thursday.

The EPA said Thursday it does not comment on pending litigation. However, it said in announcing the repeal that it would save the industry more than $300bn in costs and help “unleash” American energy. EPA assistant administrator Aaron Szabo said in September that it will allow utilities to “make the best decision for the ratepayers based on cost and cost savings, instead of being required to shut down facilities”.

The coalition is petitioning the US court of appeals for the District of Columbia to review the EPA’s decision and strike down the repeal. It says the EPA unlawfully abandoned the pollution limits without properly considering reasonable alternatives or the enormous health and climate costs of allowing more pollution into the atmosphere. The coalition also told the EPA it intends to sue over the agency’s failure to regulate pollution from many gas-fired power plants.

The suit comes as the supreme court prepares to hear a landmark case in which the city and county of Boulder, Colorado, are suing oil and gas companies to force them to help pay for damage caused by disasters linked to climate change.
The case is part of a wave of climate change litigation around the country and the world with billions of dollars at stake. The high court will hear the case on Monday, the first day of its new term.

The rule change for power plants, first proposed last year, represents a fundamental shift from efforts by Democrats Joe Biden and Barack Obama to address climate change and regulate carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases that trap the sun’s heat. Environmental groups say it will come at a cost to Americans’ health and further degrade the environment.

The separate rule proposed last month could prevent future administrations from regulating greenhouse gas emissions from power plants. The proposal, expected to be made final next year, follows EPA’s action earlier this year revoking a scientific finding that long has been the central basis for US action to regulate greenhouse gas emissions and fight climate change.

The coalition includes the states of New York, Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, North Carolina, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Washington and Wisconsin.

articles.title: Klopp wins first game as Germany coach, without 'top dogs'
articles.summary: It may have taken a little longer than he would have liked, but Jürgen Klopp has finally won a game as Germany coach. Despite a number of debutants, it was a familiar face who stood out in the…

image.caption: Jürgen Klopp has won his first game as Germany boss, after replacing Julian Nagelsmann after the World CupImage: Tom Weller/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: After 47 days, three matches and 44 squad players, Jürgen Klopp has a first win as coach of Germany's men's fotball team. A straightforward 2-0 victory over Serbia in the Nations League on Thursday meant the former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund coach avoided becoming the first Germany boss to win any of his first three games.
"I'm really happy today," Klopp told German public broadcaster ZDF. "We were outstanding when defending and when we had the ball. We simply played wonderful football."

Klopp had raised a few eyebrows by naming two squads for the four fixtures in this extended international window. But after a somewhat fortunate draw against the Netherlands and a shock loss to Greece with the more senior of the squads, it was left to those lower down the pecking order to get things going Thursday in Munich.
Bischof gets first goal on home turf

That meant a completely new starting XI and debuts to ‌goalkeeper Jonas Urbig ⁠and ⁠winger Derry Scherhant. Such players should "develop without the top dogs" Klopp said before the game. And while Urbig was untroubled by Serbia, his Bayern Munich teammate Tom Bischof made his mark by turning in the opener after Florian Wirtz, one of the sprinkling of senior players, hit the post. It was Bischof's first goal for Germany in only his second national team game.

blocks.caption: Florian Wirtz (left) and Tom Bischof were Germay's goalscorersImage: Karl-Josef Hildenbrand/AFP

blocks.text: "It's indescribable," said Bischof after the game at Bayern's Allianz Arena. "The stadium was on fire. I let it all out and was overjoyed." Unfortunately, he said, "my knees hurt a little from sliding on my knees. But that doesn't matter."

After a string of tournament failures, the latest new dawn for Germany comes with a little more patience. As well as Klopp's track record, there is a general acceptance from inside the country and abroad that Germany are no longer a top tier side.
"We're not the Bayern Munich of European football," Klopp said prematch. "We're a team that needs to find its footing."
Klopp: 'I liked everything'
While one win against a limited Serbia side will not change that, the emphatic nature of the performance impressed the new boss.

"I liked everything — the opening phase, the middle section, and the end. Our counter-pressing was off the charts," said the man whose Gegenpressing (Counter-pressing) tactic became his trademark at Dortmund. "We can afford to take all the liberties and risks we want when we win the ball back together. Everyone was there during our pressing moments."

The second half brought more debuts for players who may not have made a traditional 26-man squad. Cologne winger Said El Mala and Brentford's Vitaly Janelt made their Germany bows while Celtic's Mika Baur became the country's 1,000th men's international.
It was "surreal," Baur said. "Today was a highlight for everyone, not just for me with my debut."
Wirtz provides spark and hope

While Klopp may have seen enough from a few of the second string to afford them opportunities in the future, the performance of Liverpool midfielder Wirtz, who scored Germany's second goal, may be the most critical of the night.

Wirtz, 23, has struggled to find his best form in the Premier League and has blown hot and cold in his 47 caps for Germany. A cool and composed finish suggested that the player who was so highly regarded at Bayer Leverkusen can be coaxed to life by Klopp.

"It was loads of fun. Every single one of us gave it our all on the field. We stuck to the game plan and did almost everything right," said Wirtz, who took the captain's armband later in the game. "The players around me made it easy for me. We had a lot of movement in the middle. We were all fired up."

The challenge now for Klopp is to work out which of his wide pool of players are the ones he can rely on to take Germany to Euro 2028 and beyond. The next step is a chance for revenge against Greece in Thessaloniki on Sunday.

articles.title: Proposal to hold Major League Baseball game in Grand Teton national park sparks backlash
articles.summary:
MLB reportedly contacted White House about staging game at Wyoming park, to dismay of locals and conservationists

A proposal to hold a Major…

blocks.text: A proposal to hold a Major League Baseball (MLB) game inside a national park is receiving backlash from locals and conservationists.

On 26 September, the Washington Post reported that MLB reached out to the White House about staging a one-day game at the Grand Teton national park in Wyoming. Teton county describes itself as a “a year-round resort community” and sits within the Jackson Hole valley. It’s also a habitat for grizzly bears, osprey, bison and more.

News of the MLB’s outreach to the federal government quickly sparked concern about the impact that erecting a field and the infrastructure to hold spectators could have on the natural landscape and habitat of scores of wildlife who call the 310,000-acre (125,500-hectare) park home.
The outrage over the possible MLB game comes as national parks across the US struggle under funding cuts, staffing shortages and consistent overcrowding.
A Teton county commissioner, Luther Propst, described the idea of hosting a baseball game at the park as an “incomprehensible and deeply unwelcome notion” that he will work to stop.

“We all love baseball but neither [the Grand Teton national park] nor any other national park is an appropriate venue. This is a national issue, and completely contrary to the history and mission of our national parks set aside for preservation, contemplation of the beauty of nature, and wildlife habitat,” his post read.
The National Wildlife Federation echoed these concerns in a Facebook post of its own.

“Our national parks exist to protect wildlife, preserve breathtaking landscapes and give families a chance to connect with nature – not to host corporate sporting events,” the non-profit posted on Monday. “Let’s keep our national parks wild.”
after newsletter promotion

In a statement to the Guardian, a White House spokesperson said that it was approached by the MLB about the possibility of hosting the game but the National Park Service had not granted any permits to do so and the game is not a White House directive.
Neither MLB nor the National Park Service immediately responded to the Guardian’s request for comment.

articles.title: PCG: China research vessel forced to exit Batanes waters
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) on Thursday said it was able to force a Chinese research vessel to leave an area it had occupied for four days off Batanes and within the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) on Thursday said it was able to force a Chinese research vessel to leave an area it had occupied for four days off Batanes and within the Philippine exclusive economic zone (EEZ).
The Jia Hai Ke 7 relocated from a spot 69 kilometers northwest of Itbayat, Batanes, at 11:42 a.m., said the PCG, which first sighted the craft within the EEZ on Sept. 28.
Thanks to “sustained pressure” applied by the PCG ship BRP Teresa Magbanua and an Islander aircraft, “the mission against the Chinese research vessel Jia Hai KE 7 was successful,” it said.

It was the second instance this week where the PCG said it had managed to drive out unauthorized Chinese presence from the EEZ. The first was on Monday when a Chinese maritime militia vessel and 24 sampans were ordered to leave the waters near Kota Island, one of the islands composing Palawan’s Kalayaan municipality.
Baseless claim

Thursday’s encounter also happened about three months after Chinese scholars and commentators made a claim that Batanes was part of China. The claim was roundly dismissed by Philippine officials and scholars as baseless.
Shortly before 8 a.m., the Magbanua began issuing radio challenges to the Jia Hai Ke 7. A PCG team on a rubber boat was then deployed to circle the Chinese vessel.
The PCG ship continued to shadow the Jia Hai Ke until the latter exited the Philippine EEZ, the Coast Guard said.
But before the research vessel left, a China Coast Guard vessel—CCG-2503—arrived, moved toward the Magbanua, and issued its own challenges.
The Magbanua then shadowed CCG-2503 as well from about 914 meters while staying near the research vessel.
Plan to board called off

In an interview with reporters, Rear Adm. Jay Tarriela, the PCG spokesperson on the West Philippine Sea, said the PCG initially intended to board the research vessel after learning it was privately owned and did not enjoy sovereign immunity.
In its report on the incident, the PCG asked why a Chinese law enforcement vessel entered the picture, saying it raised questions over Jia Hai Ke 7’s purpose and principal.
The PCG raised the possibility that the research vessel was collecting data on undersea cable corridors in the Luzon Strait.

“A vessel exercising innocent passage or freedom of navigation would proceed on its course. JIA HAI KE 7 has instead held its position in the same waters for four days, which is a clear indication that it is conducting MSR (marine scientific research),” the PCG said.
Tarriela added: ‘’What was (its) real objective in going to Batanes? That is something the Chinese Embassy has to explain.’’
Embassy cries interference
The Chinese Embassy rejected the PCG’s account and accused the latter of harassing the Chinese vessel.

Deputy spokesperson Guo Wei said Jia Hai Ke 7 was conducting “normal operations” in waters that Beijing considers under its jurisdiction, and that its activities were consistent with international law, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea.
Guo accused the PCG of infringing on Beijing’s sovereign rights and jurisdiction in the area and of endangering Chinese vessels and personnel.
He also called on the Philippines to restrain its military and law enforcement agencies, and to stop interfering in China’s scientific research activities. /cb

articles.title: Tennessee suspends executions as Christa Pike’s lawyer says failed lethal injection leaves her in critical condition
articles.summary: Independent inquiry ordered after failed execution of Pike, who was convicted of 1994 murder

blocks.text: Tennessee’s governor on Thursday said it was “deeply disturbing” that his state botched the execution of a death row prisoner who remained alive and snoring 40 minutes after receiving a double dose of the lethal drug that should have quickly killed her.

Bill Lee, a Republican, has suspended all executions in the state until at least the end of the year and ordered an independent inquiry after Wednesday night’s failed attempt to put to death Christa Pike, who was convicted of murder, at the execution chamber in Nashville.

Meanwhile, Pike, 50, remained in the hospital on Thursday afternoon. “We don’t have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment, but we do know that she is alive right now and receiving life-saving medical care,” Randy Spivey, one of her attorneys, said at an afternoon press conference.
“She is in critical condition receiving life-saving care. That is the extent of what we have at the moment.”

Spivey, of the office of the post-conviction defender, condemned Tennessee authorities for the manner in which the failed attempt unfolded. He said officials used seven needles, one of which became bent as it was removed from Pike’s arm.

“Last night was not just inefficient, it was cruel and it was torturous. It was also predictable,” he said, adding that he saw no life-saving care given after the execution attempt was abandoned at about 8.25pm.

Speaking to reporters on Thursday morning, Lee said he had spoken with Frank Strada, secretary of the Tennessee department of correction, but did not have an update on the condition of Pike, who was taken to an off-site medical facility after surviving two doses of pentobarbital.

“This is a tragedy,” Lee said, adding that he had not yet spoken to the families of Pike or the teenager she killed in 1995. “There is no one that wanted what happened last night to happen. It shouldn’t have happened.

“It’s the most difficult of circumstances as it relates to the sentence that should have been carried out by the state. It’s a tragedy, and it’s deeply disturbing that that has happened in this state. The people deserve better than that.”
Lee added, in comments reported by the Tennessean, that he had not yet chosen an investigator to lead a “comprehensive, third party review” he announced in a statement late Wednesday.
“There are a lot of questions,” he said. “The people of our state deserve to have those questions answered. I’m highly disappointed, along with Tennesseans, about what happened.”

Cameron Sexton, the Republican speaker of Tennessee’s house of representatives, said on Thursday in a social media post that he and other lawmakers would also be investigating what went wrong with the attempted execution. He added that they would look at other ways to prevent executions from failing.
“We will look at all options – expanding the alternatives, and changing the current medications to include potassium chloride,” he said. “Thirty years is too long for justice.”

Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said her group was aware of seven other people that have survived medical problems due to an execution team’s failure to access a vein to administer lethal injection drugs, but nobody had remained alive after receiving the drugs used in such executions.
“This failed attempt is the worst we’ve ever seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era,” she said in a statement.

“What happened to Christa Pike can be attributed to the extreme secrecy Tennessee officials have maintained about their execution procedures, their refusal to answer reasonable questions and their unwillingness to accept responsibility for their mistakes.”
In May, Tennessee officials called off the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers, another convicted murderer, after failing for more than an hour to place an intravenous line into his arm.
Pike, who was sentenced to death for the brutal 1994 killing of a teenage classmate, was set to be the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.

The execution attempt was allowed to proceed only after the US supreme court intervened late on Wednesday to lift a federal court stay issued earlier in the day, a delay it said was necessary to assess whether Pike’s allegations of childhood sexual abuse were fully considered at her 1996 sentencing.

Lawyers for Pike filed an emergency motion to the Tennessee supreme court after the second pentobarbital dose was administered asking to halt and stay the execution, saying she was in “unnecessary agony”, and that the state was violating her right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment.
A representative of the state corrections department defended its handling of the unsuccessful execution attempt.

“The Tennessee Department of Correction followed every step of the State’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office,” the spokesperson, Dorinda Carter, said in a statement.

“The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening. Christa Pike has been transported to an off-site medical facility.”

According to the AP, Tennessee’s execution protocol calls for a secondary set of drug syringes to be administered “if the inmate is not deceased” after the first set. It does not spell out what happens if the subject is alive after the second set.

Seven journalists who were present at the Riverbend maximum security institution as witnesses described what they saw during a livestream hosted by WVLT television station soon after curtains in the execution chamber were lowered for the final time.
They said Pike was snoring as corrections officials escorted them out.
John North, of ABC News affiliate WBIR, said: “It appears this did not go how this was supposed to go. When we left the building, so far as we knew, she was probably still alive.”

Pike and her boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp were 18 and 17 when they and another female friend tortured and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, one of their classmates at Knoxville Job Corps, in January 1995, using boxcutters and a rock.

The case garnered nationwide headlines due to the ages of those involved and the brutality of the murder, in which Shipp carved a pentagram into their victim’s chest and Pike later showed a friend a fragment of her skull.
Pike never denied the killing, and was later diagnosed with mental health disorders.
“I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” she said in a clemency petition that Lee and the US supreme court denied.

Lee’s suspension order affects the only other execution set in Tennessee this year. Gary Wayne Sutton has been on death row since 1996 for the murder of a friend, and was scheduled to be put to death on 3 December.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: UK airlines to be banned from charging parents to sit with children
articles.summary:
Planned rule change forms part of Burnham’s bid to crack down on the ‘little charges that add up’

Airlines will be blocked from charging parents extra to sit with their children on planes,…

blocks.text: Airlines will be blocked from charging parents extra to sit with their children on planes, according to government plans.

The new rule would require airlines to seat passengers aged under 14 next to their parents or an accompanying adult free of charge. Passengers will also no longer need to pay to tweak the name on their flight booking if they need to correct a mistake.

It is understood that ministers will try to introduce the changes before the start of next year’s summer holidays. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said the rule changes are part of a crackdown on the “little charges that add up” when families plan their holidays.

MPs are in the process of debating a new set of rules for travel companies, as the civil aviation (consumer protection and regulatory reform) bill makes its way through parliament. The proposed law will give ministers flexible power to set out passenger rights and the duties of airlines and airports.
Burnham said: “Charging parents just to sit with their children is a rip-off, plain and simple. And being hit with a hefty fee for a simple spelling mistake on a booking form isn’t right either.

“People are fed up with these little charges that add up, so I’m putting a stop to them. This is what our everyday fixes are all about – giving people room to breathe by tackling the small irritations that catch people out, waste their time and cost them money.”
An arrangement to sit together can currently cost a parent and child up to £104 on a return journey, according to the Department for Transport.

Rory Boland, editor of consumer magazine Which? Travel, said: “It’s clearly unfair to force parents and children as young as three to pay an extra fee just to sit together. Airlines that have separated families are putting profit ahead of passenger peace of mind.”

Earlier this year, Ryanair adjusted its family seating policy after an investigation was launched into the company charging parents to sit with their children on flights. The Irish operator previously required parents travelling with children aged between two and 11 to pay to reserve what was referred to as a mandatory family seat.

Children were then allocated seats next to or near parents free of charge. The fee for a mandatory family seat was typically about £8 each way, the UK Competition and Markets Authority watchdog found.
after newsletter promotion
Under the new policy, parents will still have the option of paying to reserve a seat of their choosing and have their children alongside them free of charge.

The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, has also announced a crackdown on bad behaviour by passengers on aircraft, with the government, airlines and trade unions working on a new system for sharing information about disruptive passengers.
Airlines logged more than 1,000 serious disruptive passenger incidents in 2025, government figures show, including what it described as a mid-air brawl that caused a flight to be diverted.
Using the new system, airlines could choose to ban persistently disruptive passengers from their aircraft.

articles.title: U.K. counter-terror police arrest British-Iranian suspect over Fairford air base investigation
articles.summary: British counter-terrorism police investigating a suspected plot involving an air base used by the U.S. ‌to target Iran said on Thursday they had arrested a dual UK-Iranian national on suspicion of…

image.caption: The entrance to the RAF Fairford air base is seen in Fairford, England, on Thursday. (David Bown/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New

British counter-terrorism police investigating a suspected plot involving an air base used by the U.S. ‌to target Iran said on Thursday they had arrested a dual UK-Iranian national on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts.
5 men previously arrested but later released over accusations of bombing plot

British counter-terrorism police investigating a suspected plot involving an air base used by the U.S. ‌to target Iran said on Thursday they had arrested a dual U.K.-Iranian national on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts.

In an incident that triggered a major police response, raised alarm among Western allies and remains largely unexplained, five ​British men in their 20s were arrested Sunday near RAF Fairford in western England ​on suspicion of terrorism and explosives offences.

The men were later released without charge on police bail. But counter-terrorism police ​said they were investigating whether a foreign state had been involved, and ⁠Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Wednesday ‌the incident might have had an Iranian link.
Iran has said accusations that it was involved are baseless and on Thursday summoned the British ambassador in Tehran over the issue.
In the latest development, police said they had arrested the 25-year-old dual national ⁠in London.

"The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of enquiry," Britain's senior national co-ordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, Vicki Evans, ‌said in a statement.
"As we've made clear, we're looking at all possible angles — including possible foreign state involvement."

items: British police say no explosives found in vehicles near U.S.-run base

blocks.text: Police launched a major operation early Sunday "due to a range of information" including an alert from a local ​farmer who became suspicious after seeing the men near the base in three vans.
However, the Times ⁠reported that one of the men had also called emergency services shortly before ⁠being arrested.
Detectives have confirmed that although petrol was found in the vans used by the ⁠men, ⁠no improvised explosive device was found.

Burnham ​said Britain was working closely with the U.S., whose bombers have in recent months used ​Fairford to launch missions against ⁠Iran. U.S. President Donald Trump said he would not have released the men, whom police said were only freed under stringent conditions.
Trump previously said those involved had planned "big damage" while U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio also pointed to the "hands of a foreign actor" in the ⁠incident.

articles.title: Rapper Rick Ross arrested, charged with battery and accused of domestic violence
articles.summary: Rapper Rick Ross was arrested in Miami Beach on Thursday and charged with domestic violence following an alleged incident, local authorities confirmed to The Associated Press. Ross says he is…

image.caption: Rapper Rick Ross is shown in this booking photo provided by the Miami-Dade County Corrections and Rehabilitation after his arrest for battery on Thursday. Ross says he is innocent and the accusations are 'fabricated allegations.' (Miami-Dade County Corrections and Rehabilitation/The Associated Press

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

Rapper Rick Ross was arrested in Miami Beach on Thursday and charged with domestic violence following an alleged incident, local authorities confirmed to The Associated Press. Ross says he is innocent and the accusations are 'fabricated allegations.'
An arraignment is set for Oct. 22 in Miami
WARNING: This article may affect those who have experienced​ ​​​intimate partner violence or know someone affected by it.
American rapper Rick Ross was arrested in Miami Beach on Thursday and charged with battery in relation to an alleged domestic violence incident, local authorities confirmed to The Associated Press.

Ross, whose legal name is William Roberts II, is facing one felony count of battery by strangulation and one misdemeanor battery charge and was released from jail on a cash bond, according to online court records.

Reports say an unidentified woman told local detectives she'd been living with Ross when on Aug. 28 she alleges he accused her of cheating on him and struck her multiple times. She also alleges Ross choked her with her shirt collar and slammed her into a wall.
A report was filed Tuesday and Ross surrendered himself at the local police station Thursday morning.
In an Instagram story posted Thursday from a car, Ross repeatedly claimed he is innocent and referred to the accusations as "fabricated allegations."
In a statement to CBC News, legal representatives for Ross maintain his innocence and say that the rapper has pled not guilty to both charges.

"He respectfully requests that his friends, fans and the general public not prejudge the situation and allow the judicial process to run its course," his defence attorneys Steve Sadow and Bradley Horenstein wrote in an email.
Ross became a well-known Miami-based rapper in the 2000s, rising to fame with his 2006 debut single Hustlin' and eventually singing with Jay Z's label Def Jam Records.
His first album Port of Miami debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 chart. In 2008, he founded his own label Maybach Music Group, signing artists like Meek Mill and French Montana.
An arraignment for the case is scheduled for Oct. 22.

If you’re in immediate danger or fear for your safety or that of others around you, please call 911. If you’re affected by family or intimate partner violence, you can look for help through crisis lines and local support services.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Griffin Jaeger is a reporter and producer with CBC's entertainment unit. He also formerly hosted and produced content for The National’s digital platforms. You can reach him at griffin.jaeger@cbc.ca
